title: RetailAgentOS WebMCP Agent Storefront
pitch: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers.
about_excerpt: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers. RetailAgentOS's deterministic engine decides what that action is Inspiration I did not start RetailAgentOS to build another shopping demo. I started it because the next interface to commerce will increasingly be an AI agent—and small retailers should not be left behind. My goal is to make agentic commerce accessible to every retailer, from a solo merchant to a global enterprise. Today, becoming "agent-ready" can require specialized engineers, custom integrations, and infrastructure that only large companies can afford. If that remains true, AI commerce will widen the gap between large platforms and the millions of independent retailers that make local commerce unique. I have a direct view of that asymmetry. By day, I lead engineering for one of the largest retail storefronts in the United States, where I have spent years working on the kinds of systems I am describing here: eligibility rules, inventory truth, fulfillment feasibility, promotion stacking, and the pricing context that determines what a given shopper may actually buy. At that scale, the reasoning layer exists—but it is distributed across backend services, much of it is enforced late in the journey, it is expensive to build, and it was designed for one company. Rebuilding another bespoke stack for another large retailer is not the interesting problem. Making these capabilities accessible to an independent merchant is. RetailAgentOS is my independent work. It is informed by my professional experience and general retail-engineering patterns, but it uses no proprietary employer code, data, architecture, or confidential information and does not imply employer sponsorship or endorsement. RetailAgentOS is my attempt to close that gap through an open-source platform. A retailer should be able to describe its products and selling rules once—inventory, pricing, eligibility, delivery, substitutions, customization, and quote policies—and let different AI agents interact with the business accurately and safely. I released RetailAgentOS under the Apache 2.0 license. Its specifications are published as versioned RFCs with their open questions left intact, and the specifications ship alongside a runnable reference implementation—so the rules a retailer reads are the rules the engine actually executes. That mission shaped the retailers I chose for this showcase. Fresh Corner Market represents the neighborhood grocery store: the kirana store found throughout India and South Asia, the neighborhood shop found across Europe, or the independent corner market serving communities in the United States. These stores operate with changing local inventory, narrow delivery windows, substitutions, and close customer relationships. Their commerce rules may look simple on a webpage, but they are highly contextual. An AI agent must know when inventory cannot be trusted, offer an acceptable substitute, and preserve the shopper's control. TheCustomHub represents another important small-retailer model: a specialized American business selling customized apparel. It is also the first real retailer working with me to explore how RetailAgentOS can support an operating business. Its transactions cannot always be reduced to "add item to cart." A request may include color, youth-size quantities, artwork, budget, and delivery requirements that a merchant must review before providing a price. The challenge demo uses an authorized controlled fixture—not a live production backend—but it reflects the real quote-first workflow RetailAgentOS is being designed to support. These two retailers were chosen deliberately. One needs an agent to recover a simple grocery cart when inventory is uncertain. The other needs an agent to preserve a complex custom order without fabricating a price. Together, they demonstrate why agentic commerce needs to support the diversity of real retail—not force every retailer into the operating model of a large marketplace. WebMCP made this vision tangible. It allows the retailer's own website to expose structured actions directly to an AI agent—no marketplace intermediary and no bespoke integration for every agent. RetailAgentOS determines what is valid; WebMCP exposes only the next action the retailer can safely honor; and the human shopper retains control over consequential decisions. The long-term vision is universal access: an open foundation that lets any retailer participate in agentic commerce without surrendering its policies, customer relationships, or independence. What it does RetailAgentOS is the merchant-controlled reasoning layer. WebMCP is the browser action surface. An agent can invoke only the next commerce capability the retailer can safely honor at that moment—and which tools exist changes as the engine evaluates inventory, price, fulfillment, policy, and shopper approval. The grocery mission. A shopper asks for a weekend breakfast cart under $30 from Fresh Corner Market, with Farm Eggs and Artisan Sourdough Bread. The eggs return STOCK_STALE , so cart preparation is not merely disabled in the interface—it is not registered as a tool at all . The engine proposes Cage-Free Eggs, explains the $0.50 difference and the equivalent local delivery, and stops. A human clicks Approve. Only then does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 review cart. An optional revision to two loaves lands at $24.49, leaving $5.51 of the budget. Checkout is never registered anywhere in this showcase. The custom-order mission. Twenty-five black robotics-team shirts—six Youth Small, eleven Youth Medium, and eight Youth Large—with a one-color front logo, requested within fifteen days against a $500 ceiling. The plan reaches QUOTE_REQUIRED , which dynamically exposes request_quote . The structured request preserves every constraint the shopper stated and returns fixedPrice: null and deliveryPromise: null . The agent does not get to invent a price the merchant never set. No cart, order, payment, or checkout is created. That second mission matters most to me. Refusing to fabricate a price is not a limitation to apologize for—it is the feature that allows quote-first merchants to exist in an agentic world at all. How I built it The deterministic engine came first and predates this challenge. video_transcript_excerpt: Retailers are about to have customers who are not people. They're agents. Today those agents shop by scraping pages and guessing at stock, prices, and delivery promises no merchant ever agreed to. Retail Agent OS answers a single question deterministically. What can this retailer actually promise right now? We already had the engine. What we lacked was a way to make an agent respect it. That is what Web MCP changes. Merchant can stop being a polite advice a model can ignore and becomes a hard capability boundary inside the browser. The agent does not decide what it is allowed to do. The store does. The storefront registers its tools with the browser through Web MCP. Three to start. Capabilities, catalog search, and plan evaluation. Not search and buy. Search and plan. Checkout isn't among them. It is simply never registered. An agent cannot call a tool that does not exist. The agent reads the storefront capabilities, searches the catalog, and submits a plan for evaluation. Retail Agent OS refuses it. The inventory on those eggs is stale. So, no card gets billed on a promise the retailer can't keep. It does not simply fail though. The engine returns a substitute that merchant has already approved and registers two repair capabilities that did not exist a moment earlier. The agent's option changed because the decision changed. Applying the substitution requires a person, a real approval. Never inferred, never granted by the agent on the shopper's behalf. Once approved, the repair tools are withdrawn and cart preparation is registered. The engine re-evaluates everything from scratch. Price, inventory, delivery mode, and the shopper's budget before a cart exists at all. And the missions ends at a cart for review. Checkout was never on the table. A second storefront shows the same engine drawing a very different boundary. Custom merchandise has no valid fixed price, so no cart tool is offered at all. Only a quote request routed to the merchant review filled with customization and size information. The agent can't invent a number the merchant never set. And all of it is auditable. The tools retail agent always track against the tool the browser actually observed, plus a full registration and invocation log. And that's the bit. Retail policy that agents can't route around expressed as a life capability surface. Every retailer decides what an agent may do in their store, and the browser enforces it.
